The striped weakfish, Cynoscion guatucupa, a commercially important sciaenid inhabiting the coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic, exhibits life-history traits typical of a medium-sized, iteroparous teleost. Field studies conducted off the coast of Uruguay have provided detailed estimates of its asymptotic size and reproductive parameters. The ultimate total length that individuals can attain is estimated at 57.5 centimeters [Li = 57.5 centimeters], a value derived from length-frequency analysis of specimens collected over multiple years. This species displays a relatively slow approach to its maximum size, reflecting the energetic demands of its piscivorous diet and the seasonal productivity of its temperate habitat. Such a length-based asymptotic measure is consistent with values reported for other congeneric species such as Cynoscion regalis, though C. guatucupa appears to reach a slightly smaller ultimate size, which may be linked to latitudinal differences in thermal regimes and prey availability. The length-mass relationship, calculated as W = 0.00776 × L^3.06, allows conversion between these key morphological metrics and provides a basis for estimating body condition and reproductive output across the population.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, female striped weakfish exhibit a clearly defined total length at puberty of 34.6 centimeters [Lp = 34.6 centimeters], a benchmark that is critically important for fisheries management and the establishment of minimum catch sizes. This length corresponds to the point at which 50% of females in the population are estimated to have initiated gonadal development, based on macroscopic and histological examination of ovarian tissue. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is estimated at 398 grams [Wwp = 398 grams], a mass that reflects the energetic investment necessary to support initial vitellogenesis and the onset of spawning activity. Individuals below this size threshold are rarely found with developing oocytes, indicating a clear size-based transition to reproductive competence. This length at puberty is somewhat smaller than comparable values reported for the congeneric Cynoscion nebulosus, a pattern that may be linked to differences in growth rate and mortality regimes between estuarine and more open-coastal environments. Such life-history benchmarks are essential for constructing age-structured population models and for evaluating the impacts of fishing pressure on the reproductive potential of the stock.

During the peak of the spawning season, which occurs in the austral spring and summer months, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a mean value of 3% [GSI = 3%] when measured at a water temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C].

Reproductive output begins with the production of small, pelagic eggs, and the initial investment at the individual level is captured by the wet weight at birth. Based on an egg diameter of 0.72 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams], reflecting the minute size of the fertilized ovum that disperses into the water column. This extremely small birth mass is typical of marine teleosts that produce numerous small eggs as part of a high-fecundity, low-survival reproductive strategy. The egg itself is spherical and transparent, with a single oil globule, and its density ensures neutral buoyancy at salinities typical of the continental shelf. The larval stage that emerges after eclosion is a yolk-sac larva that remains lecithotrophic for a brief period before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that depends on the availability of suitable microzooplanktonic prey. Given the small size of the newly hatched larva, first feeding success is highly sensitive to environmental conditions, and mortality rates during this early planktonic phase are substantial, as is common among pelagic spawners with a dispersive larval ecology.

The ultimate wet weight reached by adult striped weakfish provides a measure of the maximum somatic size that can be achieved under prevailing environmental conditions. Calculated from the length-mass relationship applied to the asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight is estimated at 1881 grams [Wwi = 1881 grams], representing the ceiling of body mass for this species in the wild. This value corresponds to individuals that have completed their somatic growth trajectory and are investing energy primarily in reproductive efforts and maintenance of body condition. The complete life cycle, from fertilized egg to natural death, unfolds over a maximum lifespan estimated at 8395 days [am = 8395 days] for populations inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 17.2 °C at a temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years], places Cynoscion guatucupa among the longer-lived members of the Sciaenidae, a trait that confers a degree of demographic buffering against years of poor recruitment at a temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C].
